sections.title: Introduction to Level 3 Input Output
sections.content: In Level 3, the machine does not only perform sorting but also applies complex logical operations. These may include box-based calculations, matrix-style transformations, and multiple-step logic. In each step, the new value is often derived from the previous step, so analyzing consecutive steps carefully is essential to understand the pattern.

sections.title: Concept of Box-Based Input Output
sections.content:
In this type of question, numbers are placed in separate boxes, and in the next step mathematical operations are performed between these boxes to produce new values. Often adjacent boxes are combined by adding, subtracting, or taking the sum of digits. Example: Input Boxes: [23] [45] [67]
Step 1: 2+3 = 5, 4+5 = 9, 6+7 = 13
In Step 2, new values may again be formed from these results.

sections.title: Cross-Diagonal Operations
sections.content: Cross-diagonal operations work similarly to matrix patterns. Numbers in the top row are combined diagonally. Example: If the boxes contain 12, 34, 56, 78, then diagonal pairs may be 12 with 78 or 34 with 56. Addition, subtraction, or multiplication can then be applied to these pairs.

sections.title: Nested Logic Operations
sections.content: Nested logic means that multiple operations are performed sequentially within the same step. For example: In Step 1 the difference of digits is taken. In Step 2 the square of that difference is calculated. In Step 3 the digits of the result are reversed. This sequence may be applied to each box.

sections.title: Use of Absolute Difference
sections.content: Absolute difference means that the difference between two digits is always taken as a positive value. Example: The difference between digits 8 and 3 is 5 regardless of the order. Many questions use this difference for further calculations.

sections.title: Digit Reverse Logic
sections.content: In some patterns the digits of a number are reversed. Example: Reversing 42 produces 24. This operation is often applied after performing square or sum operations.

sections.title: Identifying Multi-Step Patterns
sections.content: In Level 3 questions, identifying the pattern requires careful observation of at least 3–4 steps. Check what mathematical operation is applied to the numbers and whether the same rule repeats in each step. Sometimes the sequence of operations is also important.

sections.title: Questions Asked in Examinations
sections.content: 1. What will be the result after Step 3 or Step 4? 2. Which number will appear in the final row? 3. What will be the value of a particular box? 4. What will be the next step according to the given rule?

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content: 1. Not recognizing that multiple operations are applied. 2. Forgetting to reverse digits. 3. Taking negative values incorrectly while calculating differences. 4. Misunderstanding box pairing or diagonal pairing.

sections.title: Quick Summary
sections.content: Level 3 Input Output patterns often involve box calculations, cross-diagonal combinations, and nested mathematical operations. Each step usually depends on the previous step, so analyzing consecutive steps carefully is the most important strategy.

tricks.title: Box Pairing Identification Trick
tricks.explanation: If the number of boxes decreases in the next step, it is likely that two boxes are combined to create a new value.

tricks.title: Digit Sum Shortcut
tricks.explanation: If a large number suddenly becomes smaller, the sum of its digits might have been taken.

tricks.title: Absolute Difference Recognition
tricks.explanation: If the difference between two digits is used, the negative value is treated as positive.

tricks.title: Square Pattern Recognition
tricks.explanation: If numbers increase rapidly, the square of a difference or sum might be taken.

tricks.title: Digit Reverse Recognition
tricks.explanation: If a number appears reversed, the digits may have been reversed.

tricks.title: Diagonal Pair Trick
tricks.explanation: In matrix-style inputs, the first and last numbers or cross pairs are often combined.

tricks.title: Step Sequence Method
tricks.explanation: Write the pattern separately from Input to Step 1 and from Step 1 to Step 2. This makes the sequence of operations clearer.
tricks.example:
Step 1: difference
Step 2: square
Step 3: reverse

tricks.title: Box Reduction Rule
tricks.explanation: If the number of boxes decreases by one in each step, adjacent boxes are being combined.

tricks.title: Operation Order Identification
tricks.explanation: In nested logic, the order of operations is very important. For example, first difference, then square, and finally reverse.

tricks.title: Final Output Estimation
tricks.explanation: Once the pattern becomes clear, apply each step mentally to quickly determine the final row.
